title: End-to-End Quantum Key Distribution Across Hybrid Fiber and Free-Space Links with All-Optical Encoding Conversion
authors: Khen Cohen, Tomer Nahum, Michael Tzukran, Paz Or, Yehuda Pilnyak, Nitzan Livneh, Hagai Eisenberg, Yaron Oz, Haim Suchowski
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) promises information-theoretically secure communication, but future networks must bridge fiber and free-space links that naturally employ different photonic encodings, namely time-bin in fiber and polarization in free space. Here we demonstrate a complete hybrid fiber and free-space QKD link that bridges both media within a single end-to-end protocol, converting between the two encodings entirely in the optical domain. Using the decoy-state BB84 protocol operating at 1550 nm, we demonstrate continuous secure-key generation over a 90 m outdoor free-space link. The system operates across atmospheric conditions spanning more than two orders of magnitude in the refractive-index structure parameter Cn^2, from strong daytime turbulence to quiescent nighttime conditions, and we further validate photon-level operation over a 750 m free-space extension. Throughout, the link maintains a session-mean quantum bit error rate (QBER) of 5.6-6.8%, well below the 11% BB84 security threshold. The encoding conversion is performed entirely in the optical domain without measurement or state reconstruction, preserving the security assumptions of the BB84 protocol. Consequently, the time-bin-to-polarization (T2P) and polarization-to-time-bin (P2T) converters remain part of the untrusted quantum channel rather than trusted intermediate nodes. These results establish secure photonic encoding conversion as a practical interface between fiber and free-space quantum communication platforms, providing a building block for future quantum networks applications.
summary: The paper demonstrates a functional, end-to-end Quantum Key Distribution link bridging optical fiber and free-space channels using an all-optical time-bin to polarization encoding converter. By maintaining low error rates across varying atmospheric turbulence conditions, the research establishes a crucial building block for realizing practical quantum networks that span terrestrial and open-air links.
main_problem: The core challenge is establishing end-to-end Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) across hybrid links that combine optical fiber and free-space channels, which inherently use different photonic encodings.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated continuous secure key generation over a 90 m hybrid link under varying atmospheric conditions while maintaining a low QBER below the security threshold. This establishes a practical, all-optical interface for future quantum networks.
method: They employed the decoy-state BB84 protocol and developed an end-to-end system incorporating specialized optical converters to perform encoding conversion entirely in the optical domain without measurement.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a hybrid QKD link tested on an urban rooftop, connecting fiber (time-bin encoding) to free space (polarization encoding). The system operates at 1550 nm and was characterized across diurnal cycles and extended distances up to 750 m.
key_observables: Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER), secure key rate (peaking around 1.27 kbps in the Sunset session), and atmospheric turbulence metrics ($C_n^2$, $\sigma_R^2$).
important_parameters: The system maintained QBER below 7% across conditions spanning more than two orders of magnitude in $C_n^2$. The conversion stages introduce measurable optical losses ($\sim 3 	ext{ dB}$ per stage).
main_assumptions: The T2P and P2T converters are treated as untrusted components, which preserves the security assumptions of the BB84 protocol. Turbulence models rely on estimating $C_n^2$ from surface-layer measurements.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the hybrid architecture (Alice $ightarrow$ Converter $ightarrow$ Free Space $ightarrow$ Converter $ightarrow$ Bob) and show QBER vs. atmospheric turbulence strength, confirming performance stability below the security threshold.
paper_structure: The paper details the experimental setup for a hybrid link, characterizes performance across Day/Sunset/Night sessions by monitoring QBER against environmental parameters ($C_n^2$), analyzes the physical limitations imposed by free-space propagation and conversion losses, and finally calculates the secure key rate using established GLLP protocols.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical engineering bottleneck in quantum networking: interfacing disparate physical media. The all-optical encoding conversion mechanism is highly relevant for building scalable quantum internet infrastructure that must traverse diverse environments.
